docs.text: Configuring an analysis Your run configuration tells SpectroMesa-DIA where to find your inputs, how to analyze them, and where to save the results. Start from the supplied template, fill in your paths, and review the scientific settings for your experiment. This guide focuses on the settings you are most likely to change. For the full parameter tables and an explanation of each step, see the pipeline reference . Create a run configuration Create a dedicated directory for your analysis and copy the installed pipeline's template into it. Replace these example paths with your own: mkdir -p /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort cp /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/config/template.config run.config Use this analysis directory when launching and resuming the run. Nextflow finds the pipeline through the path supplied to nextflow run , so you can keep the pipeline installation separate. Open run.config in a text editor. Shared settings, such as input_csv and output_dir , belong directly inside params . The template groups the remaining settings by analysis step. Edit search settings in the MSFragger block under search_ProteomicDIA , and protein grouping settings under validate_ProteomicPSM . Values in quotes are text, true and false are switches, and lines beginning with // are comments. The template supplies starting analysis settings. The search reference identifies the peak-count setting that differs from the underlying default. Fill in your paths and change settings where your experiment requires it. The examples below show the matching blocks in your copied file. Keep the template's setup statements Preserve the includeConfig statements at the top and the final methods.setup() call. They load the defaults and check that your configuration is ready to use. Place your parameter changes before methods.setup() . Set inputs and outputs Use full paths for files and directories in the run configuration so their meaning does not depend on where you launch the analysis. Setting What to provide input_csv Your acquisition CSV, with valid paths to the mass spectrometry data. decoy_database The combined target-decoy FASTA, including contaminants if you added them. msfragger_executable The full path to the MSFragger JAR. output_dir The directory in which to save published results and logs. dataset_id A name for this analysis, such as human_dia_cohort . The default is cohort ; change it if you want a more descriptive name. Check that decoy_string , decoy_position , contam_string , and contam_position match your FASTA. The defaults use DECOY_ and CONTAMINANT_ , both as prefixes. Change only the values that differ from your database; the input guide uses CONTAM_ , so that example requires contam_string = 'CONTAM_' . The database preparation guide shows a matching MSPtools command and configuration. For Bruker .d input, also set diatracer_executable to the diaTracer JAR and bruker_lib_dir to the MSFragger ext/bruker directory. See Installation for the required files. Published analysis results are organized under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/main_workflow/ Execution logs are stored alongside main_workflow . Nextflow's work directory holds intermediate task files and is configured separately when launching the analysis; allow space for both work files and published results. Configure identification and protein grouping Digestion and modifications Review the search_ProteomicDIA { MSFragger { ... } } block against your sample preparation. The supplied template uses the following settings: Setting Template value Meaning search_enzyme_name_1 'stricttrypsin' The search enzyme name. search_enzyme_cut_1 'KR' Cleavage at lysine or arginine. search_enzyme_nocut_1 '' No following residue blocks cleavage in this configuration. search_enzyme_sense_1 'C' Cleavage on the C-terminal side. allowed_missed_cleavage_1 2 Allowed missed cleavages. num_enzyme_termini 2 Require two enzymatic termini. add_C_cysteine 57.02146 Fixed cysteine carbamidomethylation. variable_mod_01 '15.9949 M 3' Variable methionine oxidation. variable_mod_02 '42.0106 [^ 1' Variable protein N-terminal acetylation. max_variable_mods_per_peptide 3 Maximum variable modifications per peptide. These are starting settings, not assumptions the pipeline can infer from your data. For example, review the fixed cysteine modification if your preparation used a different alkylation chemistry. If you change the enzyme, review all of its cleavage settings together and set validate_ProteomicPSM.enzyme to the corresponding OpenMS enzyme name. Search and validation use different enzyme naming conventions. Mass tolerances The template uses these mass tolerances, all expressed in parts per million (ppm) : Tolerance Template value Settings in the MSFragger block Precursor search window −25 to +25 ppm precursor_mass_lower , precursor_mass_upper Calibrated precursor tolerance 4 ppm precursor_true_tolerance Fragment mass tolerance 50 ppm fragment_mass_tolerance Adjust these values in the MSFragger block to suit your instrument and acquisition method before running the full cohort. Protein grouping and identification thresholds ProteinProphet is selected by default. To use another method, change validate_ProteomicPSM.protein_inference_algorithm to the corresponding value: Method Configuration value ProteinProphet, the default 'ProteinProphet' Fido 'Fido' EPIFANY 'Epifany' MSBooster and Percolator validate the search results before protein grouping. Accepted identifications are then used to build the spectral library. Two relevant thresholds in validate_ProteomicPSM are: Setting Default Purpose filter_psm_score_peptide 0.01 Filtering threshold for the validated PSM output. easypqp_psm_qvalue 0.01 Maximum PSM q-value for export to spectral library generation. Protein-group export also has a method-specific minimum probability: proteinprophet_min_probability defaults to 0.0 , while fido_min_probability and epifany_min_probability default to 0.01 . Only the setting for the selected method applies. Protein-group probabilities are not FDR thresholds A minimum group probability of 0.01 is not a 1% FDR cutoff. Keep the meaning of each threshold in mind when changing identification filters or comparing protein-grouping methods. Configure quantitation and outputs The following DIA-NN settings are already supplied by default and shown in the template. Review them in the quoted 'DIA-NN' block inside quantitate_ProteomicDIA : quantitate_ProteomicDIA { 'DIA-NN' { qvalue = 0.01 matrix_qvalue = 0.01 no_ifs_removal = true no_prot_inf = true } } qvalue controls the main report precursor q-value cutoff, and matrix_qvalue controls the quantitation matrix q-value cutoff. The template also sets no_ifs_removal = true , which disables DIA-NN's fragment interference correction. Review that choice if you are changing the quantitation strategy. Retain upstream protein groups no_prot_inf defaults to true ; leave it unchanged. You do not need to add this setting yourself. This keeps DIA-NN protein inference disabled and retains the protein groups assigned by ProteinProphet, Fido, or EPIFANY. Setting it to false would allow DIA-NN to infer new protein groups. Fraction handling is derived from the acquisition CSV. You do not need to set a separate fractionation switch: the pipeline prepares the library and quantitation inputs, runs quantitation by fraction when needed, and produces sample-level quantitative outputs. QC follows quantitation, and ProteoVault database assembly is enabled by default ( run_proteovault = true ). Leave this unchanged to generate the database. To skip database assembly while retaining the analysis and QC outputs, set run_proteovault = false directly inside params . Choose the execution environment Container runtime Choose the profile matching the container runtime available on your machine: Runtime Nextflow profile option Docker -profile docker Apptainer -profile apptainer Singularity -profile singularity Select one of these profiles when launching the analysis. Your choice applies to all analysis steps. The standard profile uses Docker. Computing resources The bundled resource profiles are configured for machines with the following resources: Profile CPUs Memory pines 64 500 GB boutroslab_aws 32 128 GB Combine a resource profile with a runtime profile, for example -profile pines,apptainer . For a smaller workstation or a different cluster allocation, prepare a custom resource profile as described below. Profiles do not reserve a cluster node Request a cluster allocation with enough CPUs and memory before launching the pipeline. The profiles specify how much each analysis step can use; they do not submit a Slurm job for you. To adapt the resources, copy a bundled JSON file from config/resource_profiles/ to a directory you control, give it a name such as my_cluster.json , and adjust its max_cpus , max_memory , and the CPU and memory settings for each analysis step. Set: params.compute_profile = 'my_cluster' params.additional_resource_profile_dir = '/path/to/resource_profiles' Place these assignments before methods.setup() , then select your container profile when launching. Keep all entries in the copied JSON file, including the memory setting for search_database_MSFragger ; edit their values to fit the resources available to you. A complete example This example configures an unfractionated human DIA cohort with ProteinProphet and the database prepared in Preparing inputs . Replace the paths with your own and review the search settings for your preparation and instrument. Save the file as run.config and select the runtime and resource profiles when launching. includeConfig "${projectDir}/config/default.config" includeConfig "${projectDir}/config/methods.config" includeConfig "${projectDir}/nextflow.config" includeConfig "${projectDir}/config/profiles.config" params { // Inputs and tools input_csv = '/project/inputs/acquisitions.csv' decoy_database = '/project/database/UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta' decoy_string = 'DECOY_' decoy_position = 'prefix' contam_string = 'CONTAM_' // Matches the database prepared in the inputs guide contam_position = 'prefix' msfragger_executable = '/tools/MSFragger/MSFragger.jar' // Outputs output_dir = '/project/results' dataset_id = 'human_dia_cohort' run_proteovault = true search_ProteomicDIA { MSFragger { precursor_mass_lower = -25 // ppm precursor_mass_upper = 25 // ppm precursor_true_tolerance = 4 // ppm fragment_mass_tolerance = 50 // ppm isotope_error = '0/1/2' output_report_topN = 5 search_enzyme_name_1 = 'stricttrypsin' search_enzyme_cut_1 = 'KR' search_enzyme_nocut_1 = '' search_enzyme_sense_1 = 'C' allowed_missed_cleavage_1 = 2 num_enzyme_termini = 2 clip_nTerm_M = 1 variable_mod_01 = '15.9949 M 3' variable_mod_02 = '42.0106 [^ 1' allow_multiple_variable_mods_on_residue = 0 max_variable_mods_per_peptide = 3 digest_min_length = 7 digest_max_length = 50 digest_mass_range = '500.0 5000.0' max_fragment_charge = 2 minimum_peaks = 15 use_topN_peaks = 150 min_matched_fragments = 4 add_C_cysteine = 57.02146 } } validate_ProteomicPSM { protein_inference_algorithm = 'ProteinProphet' filter_psm_score_peptide = 0.01 easypqp_psm_qvalue = 0.01 } quantitate_ProteomicDIA { 'DIA-NN' { qvalue = 0.01 matrix_qvalue = 0.01 no_ifs_removal = true no_prot_inf = true } } } methods.setup() For Bruker diaPASEF data, point the CSV at the original .d directories and add these paths inside params : diatracer_executable = '/tools/diaTracer/diaTracer.jar' bruker_lib_dir = '/tools/MSFragger/ext/bruker' Before launching, check that your input and tool paths exist, your FASTA markers match, your search settings reflect the experiment, and your selected resource profile fits the available machine or allocation. Keep the final configuration with your analysis records.

docs.text: Running and resuming an analysis Once you have installed SpectroMesa-DIA , prepared your inputs , and created a run configuration , you can launch the analysis with Nextflow. Start with a small representative subset of your data to check the setup before processing the full cohort. Choose a work directory Nextflow stores intermediate files in a work directory, separate from the results directory specified by output_dir . Choose a location with enough space and keep it available until you have finished the analysis and no longer need to resume it. Use the same work path each time you launch or resume this analysis. In the examples below, replace /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work with a suitable location on your system. All machines running the analysis must be able to access it. Keep a stable work path between jobs Avoid using $SLURM_JOB_ID in the work path if you want to resume across cluster jobs: each job has a different ID. Also check your site's scratch retention policy. A stable path is only useful for resuming while its contents remain available. For initial planning, allow roughly 5–10 times the acquisition data size in additional free storage for intermediate files and published results. This is an estimate, not a measured guarantee; conversion, fractionation, and cohort size affect peak usage. Check storage use during your pilot run. Start an analysis On a workstation Use a dedicated directory for each analysis, such as /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort . Keep your prepared run.config there and launch Nextflow from that directory. Nextflow stores its run history and .nextflow.log there, while the pipeline itself can remain in a separate installation directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work Replace the example paths with your own. This example uses Docker; choose apptainer or singularity if that is what you installed. Review the computing resource settings to make sure the analysis fits your workstation. Keep the terminal session running until Nextflow finishes. -c selects your run configuration, -profile selects the execution environment, and -work-dir sets the intermediate-file location. The results still go to the output_dir in your configuration. On a Slurm cluster Run the analysis inside a compute allocation. For example, the following submission script requests resources matching the bundled boutroslab_aws resource profile and uses Apptainer. That profile can be used on a suitably sized node; its name does not require an AWS environment. Save this as run-dia.sh in your analysis directory, replace the paths, and adjust the time limit and any partition or account settings required by your cluster: #!/usr/bin/env bash #SBATCH --job-name=human_dia #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32 #SBATCH --mem=128G #SBATCH --time=24:00:00 #SBATCH --output=human_dia-%j.log set -euo pipefail # Load Java, Nextflow, and Apptainer here if your cluster uses modules. cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile boutroslab_aws,apptainer \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work Submit it from the same analysis directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort sbatch run-dia.sh The 24-hour limit is an example, not an expected runtime. Choose an appropriate limit for your cohort and cluster. The profile sets CPU and memory use; sbatch requests the allocation. For a different allocation, use a matching custom resource profile . Keep container images available between runs For Apptainer, use persistent image caches as described in Installation . Export those cache settings in your submission script as well. This avoids downloading and converting the same images repeatedly. Monitor progress Nextflow prints progress and any errors to the terminal. For the Slurm example, this output is saved to human_dia-<job-id>.log in the directory from which you submitted the script. The launch directory also contains .nextflow.log with more detailed messages. A stage such as searching or quantitation may take a long time without changing the top-level progress display. Check its logs before assuming that the analysis has stopped. The pipeline writes execution reports under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/ log-SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>-<timestamp>/nextflow-log/ trace.txt timeline.html report.html The HTML reports are most useful after the run finishes. They summarize task execution, timing, and resource use. Analysis stages also save their own logs alongside their outputs. A successful run exits with status 0 and has no failed tasks. On a cluster, check the job's final status as well as the Nextflow log. The presence of some result files alone does not mean the whole analysis completed successfully, because results are written as stages finish. If the run fails, read the reported error and the failed task's .command.err and .command.out files in the work directory shown by Nextflow. Correct the cause before trying to resume. Resume an interrupted run Add -resume to the original command, using the same launch directory, configuration, profiles, and work path. For the workstation example: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work \ -resume For the Slurm example, add -resume to the Nextflow command in run-dia.sh and submit the script again after the previous job has stopped. An interrupted stage starts again Resume currently works at the level of completed analysis stages. Nextflow can reuse a completed stage when its cached results are available and its inputs and settings still match. Work completed inside an unfinished stage is not automatically resumed. For example, if searching stops halfway through the cohort, expect the search stage to run again; completed earlier stages may be reused. Return to the same analysis directory when resuming, and keep its .nextflow folder and the original work directory. Published results alone are not enough to resume. Changing inputs, settings, or pipeline code can cause affected stages to run again. See Nextflow's resume documentation for the cache requirements. Plain -resume selects the most recent run. If you have launched another analysis from the same directory, list previous runs with: nextflow log Then use -resume RUN_NAME , replacing RUN_NAME with the name of the intended run. Do not start two attempts to resume the same run at once. Find your results The main analysis outputs are under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/main_workflow/ Look for the versioned quantitate-ProteomicDIA-* directory for quantitative reports and matrices, and qc-ProteomicDIA-* for QC summaries and plots. ProteoVault database assembly is enabled by default. When generated, the database is published one level above the dataset directory: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb You can load the generated DuckDB database into R and analyze the results using ProteoVaultR . Keep the run configuration and logs with your results. Once the analysis is complete, review the QC summaries before interpreting the quantitative comparisons. Retain the work directory if you expect to resume or investigate individual analysis steps.

Nextflow stores its run history and .nextflow.log there, while the pipeline itself can remain in a separate installation directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work Replace the example paths with your own. This example uses Docker; choose apptainer or singularity if that is what you installed. Review the computing resource settings to make sure the analysis fits your workstation. Keep the terminal session running until Nextflow finishes. -c selects your run configuration, -profile selects the execution environment, and -work-dir sets the intermediate-file location. The results still go to the output_dir in your configuration.
docs.title: On a workstation

docs.text: Run the analysis inside a compute allocation. For example, the following submission script requests resources matching the bundled boutroslab_aws resource profile and uses Apptainer. That profile can be used on a suitably sized node; its name does not require an AWS environment. Save this as run-dia.sh in your analysis directory, replace the paths, and adjust the time limit and any partition or account settings required by your cluster: #!/usr/bin/env bash #SBATCH --job-name=human_dia #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32 #SBATCH --mem=128G #SBATCH --time=24:00:00 #SBATCH --output=human_dia-%j.log set -euo pipefail # Load Java, Nextflow, and Apptainer here if your cluster uses modules. cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile boutroslab_aws,apptainer \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work Submit it from the same analysis directory: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort sbatch run-dia.sh The 24-hour limit is an example, not an expected runtime. Choose an appropriate limit for your cohort and cluster. The profile sets CPU and memory use; sbatch requests the allocation. For a different allocation, use a matching custom resource profile . Keep container images available between runs For Apptainer, use persistent image caches as described in Installation . Export those cache settings in your submission script as well. This avoids downloading and converting the same images repeatedly.
docs.title: On a Slurm cluster

docs.text: Nextflow prints progress and any errors to the terminal. For the Slurm example, this output is saved to human_dia-<job-id>.log in the directory from which you submitted the script. The launch directory also contains .nextflow.log with more detailed messages. A stage such as searching or quantitation may take a long time without changing the top-level progress display. Check its logs before assuming that the analysis has stopped. The pipeline writes execution reports under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/ log-SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>-<timestamp>/nextflow-log/ trace.txt timeline.html report.html The HTML reports are most useful after the run finishes. They summarize task execution, timing, and resource use. Analysis stages also save their own logs alongside their outputs. A successful run exits with status 0 and has no failed tasks. On a cluster, check the job's final status as well as the Nextflow log. The presence of some result files alone does not mean the whole analysis completed successfully, because results are written as stages finish. If the run fails, read the reported error and the failed task's .command.err and .command.out files in the work directory shown by Nextflow. Correct the cause before trying to resume.
docs.title: Monitor progress

docs.text: Add -resume to the original command, using the same launch directory, configuration, profiles, and work path. For the workstation example: cd /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow run /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA/main.nf \ -c /project/analyses/human_dia_cohort/run.config \ -profile docker \ -work-dir /scratch/your_user/human_dia_cohort/work \ -resume For the Slurm example, add -resume to the Nextflow command in run-dia.sh and submit the script again after the previous job has stopped. An interrupted stage starts again Resume currently works at the level of completed analysis stages. Nextflow can reuse a completed stage when its cached results are available and its inputs and settings still match. Work completed inside an unfinished stage is not automatically resumed. For example, if searching stops halfway through the cohort, expect the search stage to run again; completed earlier stages may be reused. Return to the same analysis directory when resuming, and keep its .nextflow folder and the original work directory. Published results alone are not enough to resume. Changing inputs, settings, or pipeline code can cause affected stages to run again. See Nextflow's resume documentation for the cache requirements. Plain -resume selects the most recent run. If you have launched another analysis from the same directory, list previous runs with: nextflow log Then use -resume RUN_NAME , replacing RUN_NAME with the name of the intended run. Do not start two attempts to resume the same run at once.
docs.title: Resume an interrupted run

docs.text: The main analysis outputs are under: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/main_workflow/ Look for the versioned quantitate-ProteomicDIA-* directory for quantitative reports and matrices, and qc-ProteomicDIA-* for QC summaries and plots. ProteoVault database assembly is enabled by default. When generated, the database is published one level above the dataset directory: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb You can load the generated DuckDB database into R and analyze the results using ProteoVaultR . Keep the run configuration and logs with your results. Once the analysis is complete, review the QC summaries before interpreting the quantitative comparisons. Retain the work directory if you expect to resume or investigate individual analysis steps.

docs.text: Preparing inputs SpectroMesa-DIA requires two main inputs: an input CSV listing your mass spectrometry acquisitions and their sample and fraction assignments, and a target-decoy protein sequence database in FASTA format. The CSV is valid only when its acquisition paths point to existing files or directories accessible to the pipeline. This guide walks through preparing the CSV and database. Software requirements, including MSFragger and the additional tools for Bruker data, are covered in Installation . Input CSV Create a CSV with one row per acquisition. Save it somewhere accessible to the machine running the pipeline, and use its path for input_csv in your run configuration. Columns Column What to enter sample_name The sample identifier used to group acquisitions for analysis. Repeat it for all fractions of the same sample, but give each biological or technical replicate a unique name. fraction_id A fraction identifier. For unfractionated data, use the same value, such as 1 , for every sample. annotation_id Usually the species name, such as human or mouse . This field is not currently used, but please include it. path The path to the acquisition file, or to the complete Bruker .d directory. scan Required for SCIEX .wiff acquisitions: the path to the companion .wiff.scan file. Leave it empty for other formats, or omit the column if there are no WIFF files. The first four columns are required, and their values must not be empty. Additional columns are allowed but ignored. Give technical replicates unique sample names Files with the same sample_name are treated as one sample. Their search results are combined, false discovery rate (FDR) control is performed at the sample level, and the final quantitation matrix contains one column per sample. For technical replicates, use unique names such as sample_01_rep1 and sample_01_rep2 so that they remain separate samples in the analysis and output. For a fractionated technical replicate, use its unique name for all of its fractions. Unfractionated experiments Use one row per sample, with a shared fraction identifier: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path sample_01,1,human,/data/sample_01.raw sample_02,1,human,/data/sample_02.raw Fractionated experiments Repeat each sample name across its fractions, and use consistent identifiers for corresponding fractions across samples: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path sample_01,1,human,/data/sample_01_fraction_1.mzML sample_01,2,human,/data/sample_01_fraction_2.mzML sample_02,1,human,/data/sample_02_fraction_1.mzML sample_02,2,human,/data/sample_02_fraction_2.mzML Each sample/fraction pair must be unique. The pipeline detects fractionation when the table contains more than one distinct fraction identifier. It uses these assignments during analysis and combines the fraction-level quantitative results into sample-level outputs. Give biological and technical replicates different sample names; fraction identifiers should describe fractions of the same sample. Acquisition paths and filenames You can use absolute paths, as in the examples above, or paths relative to the directory containing the CSV. For example, if the CSV is /project/inputs/acquisitions.csv , a path value of ../data/sample_01.raw refers to /project/data/sample_01.raw . All listed files and directories must exist and be accessible during the run. List each acquisition path only once. For identifiers, use letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens, starting with a letter or number. This convention works for both file inputs and Bruker data. For acquisition files, avoid extra dots before the extension: sample_01.raw is valid, but sample.01.raw is rejected. Use distinct filenames across samples, even when the files live in different directories. File names may repeat across fractions of the same sample; the conversion stage adds fraction suffixes when needed. Bruker .d directory names must be unique across all acquisitions. Giving every acquisition a distinct name is the simplest approach. Use either acquisition files or Bruker .d directories throughout one CSV; the pipeline does not accept a mixture of these two input paths in one run. File-format support depends on the selected conversion tool. SCIEX WIFF files Supply both the .wiff file and its companion .wiff.scan file: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path,scan sample_01,1,human,/data/sample_01.wiff,/data/sample_01.wiff.scan sample_02,1,human,/data/sample_02.wiff,/data/sample_02.wiff.scan The companion must have the same filename as the acquisition with .scan appended. Its path can also be relative to the CSV directory. Bruker diaPASEF acquisitions Point to the complete .d directory, keeping its contents together: sample_name,fraction_id,annotation_id,path sample_01,1,human,/data/sample_01.d sample_02,1,human,/data/sample_02.d The pipeline reconstructs spectra for identification and library generation, while DIA-NN uses the original .d acquisitions for quantitation. Keep those directories available throughout the analysis. Protein sequence database Choose a reference proteome For a typical experiment, start with the gene-centric UniProt reference proteome for the species you are studying. Use the canonical protein FASTA. For human and mouse, expect about 20,000 proteins before adding contaminants and decoys. UniProt distributes additional isoform sequences separately in files ending in _additional.fasta.gz . See the UniProt reference proteome file descriptions . Species Reference proteome Canonical protein FASTA Human UP000005640 UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz Mouse UP000000589 UP000000589_10090.fasta.gz For example, download and decompress the human reference proteome: curl -fL -o UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz \ https://ftp.uniprot.org/pub/databases/uniprot/current_release/knowledgebase/reference_proteomes/Eukaryota/UP000005640/UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz gunzip UP000005640_9606.fasta.gz Keep a record of the UniProt release and download date so you can identify the exact database used in your analysis. Choose or extend the target sequence set to match your experiment if it includes multiple species or proteins absent from the reference proteome. Add contaminants and generate decoys The pipeline requires a combined target-decoy FASTA , containing both the proteins you want to identify and decoy sequences used to estimate false discoveries. We also recommend adding common contaminant sequences so that peptides from laboratory contaminants can be assigned to those proteins. MSPtools can prepare this database in one step. No separate cRAP download needed MSPtools bundles the cRAP contaminant sequences. Use --include-crap to add them and generate their decoys along with the reference-protein decoys. After installing MSPtools, run: msptools FASTA CreateDecoyDatabase \ --input-path UP000005640_9606.fasta \ --output-path UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta \ --include-crap \ --decoy-prefix DECOY_ \ --contam-prefix CONTAM_ Start from a target-only FASTA. The resulting UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta contains the reference proteins, contaminants, and decoys for both. By default, MSPtools reverses protein sequences while preserving an initial methionine. The command shows its default prefixes, DECOY_ and CONTAM_ , explicitly. The pipeline defaults to CONTAMINANT_ for contaminants, so update that setting as shown below. Match the database markers in your run configuration Set decoy_database to the generated FASTA and check all four marker settings. For the command above, keep the default decoy_string , decoy_position , and contam_position , and change contam_string to CONTAM_ . The matching configuration is: params { decoy_database = '/path/to/UP000005640_9606-decoy_contam.fasta' decoy_string = 'DECOY_' decoy_position = 'prefix' contam_string = 'CONTAM_' contam_position = 'prefix' } Setting Meaning decoy_string The text marking decoy accessions, such as DECOY_ . decoy_position Where the decoy marker occurs. The current MSFragger workflow requires prefix . contam_string The text marking contaminant accessions. The pipeline defaults to CONTAMINANT_ ; use CONTAM_ for the example above. contam_position Where the contaminant marker occurs: prefix or suffix . Use prefix for the MSPtools command above. Match the markers in your FASTA These settings must match the markers in your FASTA accessions. A prefix appears at the beginning of the accession; a suffix appears at the end. With the example above, a contaminant accession begins with CONTAM_ , and its decoy begins with DECOY_CONTAM_ . Changing a pipeline setting does not rewrite the FASTA headers. Edit the matching settings in your copy of the pipeline's template, keeping its existing includeConfig statements and final methods.setup() call. Before you run Check that every acquisition and any required WIFF companion file is accessible from the execution environment. Check that each sample/fraction pair and acquisition path appears only once, and that annotations agree across fractions of a sample. Point input_csv to the completed CSV and decoy_database to the combined target-decoy FASTA. Confirm that the decoy and contaminant marker strings and positions match the database you generated.

docs.text: Installing SpectroMesa-DIA Requirements SpectroMesa-DIA can be run on a Linux workstation or a cluster compute node with an x86-64 processor. Before you begin, make sure you can access your mass spectrometry data and protein sequence database from that machine, and leave about 5-10x free disk or scratch space for the files the pipeline creates along the way. Install or load the following on the machine that launches the pipeline: Software Requirement Nextflow 24.10.6 with the v1 syntax parser is recommended. See below for selecting the version and parser. Container runtime Docker, Apptainer, or Singularity. Choose the runtime available on your workstation or cluster. Most analysis tools, including OpenMS, MSBooster, Percolator, EasyPQP, DIA-NN, and ProteoVault, are supplied through the configured container images. MSFragger must be obtained separately; Bruker data also require diaTracer and the Bruker reader libraries described below. Set up Nextflow We recommend Nextflow 24.10.6 . If you already have a newer Nextflow launcher installed, you can select the recommended version and syntax parser with these environment variables: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 NXF_VER selects the Nextflow version, and NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER selects its syntax parser. To use a newer version, set NXF_VER to that release and keep NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 , provided the release still supports the v1 parser. Version 24.10.6 remains our tested recommendation. If Nextflow is not installed, use the official launcher . For a user-local installation, run the following with the environment settings above already exported: mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" curl -fsSL https://get.nextflow.io -o "$HOME/.local/bin/nextflow" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/nextflow" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" nextflow -version Bruker reconstruction selects its own Nextflow version Bruker data reconstruction uses Nextflow 25.10.5, which the pipeline selects automatically. Keep your Nextflow settings as shown above, and allow Nextflow to download this additional version when it is first needed. Get the pipeline Download a release (recommended) The easiest way to get started is to download the latest release with all submodules . To download the latest release from a terminal, use either wget : wget -O source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/metapipeline-DIA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz or curl : curl -fL -o source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/metapipeline-DIA/releases/latest/download/source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz From the directory containing your download, extract it into a folder for the pipeline: mkdir -p SpectroMesa-DIA tar -xzf source_code_with_submodules.tar.gz -C SpectroMesa-DIA --strip-components=1 cd SpectroMesa-DIA You can now continue to check the container runtime . Clone with Git (alternative) If you prefer to work from a Git checkout, clone the repository with all nested submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:TheBoutrosLab/metapipeline-DIA.git SpectroMesa-DIA cd SpectroMesa-DIA The repository and its submodules use GitHub SSH URLs, so this command requires working GitHub SSH authentication and access to the repositories. To use HTTPS instead, use this alternative clone command: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ clone --recurse-submodules \ https://github.com/TheBoutrosLab/metapipeline-DIA.git SpectroMesa-DIA cd SpectroMesa-DIA For an existing checkout, initialize any missing submodules from its root: git submodule update --init --recursive When using HTTPS, apply the same command-scoped URL rewrite: git -c 'url.https://github.com/.insteadOf=git@github.com:' \ submodule update --init --recursive The submodules provide the analysis software and configuration included with this pipeline. Keep their versions matched to the pipeline checkout. Check their status with: git submodule status --recursive A leading space indicates the recorded revision is checked out. A leading - means a submodule is not initialized; + means it differs from the recorded revision. Check the container runtime Choose one runtime and use its matching Nextflow profile when launching an analysis: Runtime Check Pipeline profile Docker docker info -profile docker Apptainer apptainer --version -profile apptainer Singularity singularity --version -profile singularity Make sure Docker is running and accessible to your account, or that Apptainer or Singularity is installed on the machines where the analysis will run. The selected profile applies your choice throughout the analysis. For Apptainer, configure persistent caches before launching a run. Use directories you own that are accessible from the execution nodes: export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.cache/nextflow/apptainer" export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$HOME/.apptainer/cache" mkdir -p "$NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" "$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" Reuse container images across runs Use shared filesystem paths instead if your home directory is not available on those nodes. Both caches are relevant: some stages use Nextflow-managed images, while others use Apptainer's own image cache. Obtain MSFragger Download MSFragger through its official download instructions under the license appropriate to your use. Keep the extracted distribution in a persistent directory accessible to the analysis tasks. The pipeline requires the path to the JAR, not the containing directory. In your run configuration, set: params.msfragger_executable = '/path/to/MSFragger/MSFragger.jar' Replace the example with the actual filename, which may include a version number. The pipeline does not download this JAR for you. Additional files for Bruker diaPASEF data For .d acquisitions, also obtain the diaTracer JAR from its official repository and retain the ext/bruker directory from the compatible MSFragger distribution. Set both paths in the run configuration: params.diatracer_executable = '/path/to/diaTracer/diaTracer.jar' params.bruker_lib_dir = '/path/to/MSFragger/ext/bruker' The current reconstruction workflow expects libtimsdata-2-21-0-4.so inside that Bruker library directory. Keep the complete directory and use the actual diaTracer JAR filename. These additional files are not required for the file-input conversion route. Storage and compute environment Keep the repository, external tools, input data, and work and output directories accessible to the execution environment. Allow working storage for converted or reconstructed mzML files, copied Bruker acquisitions, intermediate results, and container images. Space requirements depend on the cohort and should not be estimated from final output size alone. Request cluster resources before launching Request a cluster allocation before launching the analysis. The bundled pines and boutroslab_aws profiles specify CPU and memory settings; they do not submit a Slurm job for you. Combine the resource and container profiles, for example -profile pines,apptainer . Verify the setup From the pipeline directory, check: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 nextflow -version test -f main.nf test -f config/template.config test -f external/search-ProteomicDIA/main.nf test -f external/validate-ProteomicPSM/main.nf test -f external/generate-ProteomicSpectralLibrary/main.nf test -f external/quantitate-ProteomicDIA/main.nf Confirm the expected Nextflow version, a working container runtime, and readable tool files. If you installed through Git, also check the submodule status as described above. The test commands produce no output when successful and return a nonzero exit status if a file is missing. These checks verify installation prerequisites; they do not run a proteomics analysis or validate all container images. docs.text: SpectroMesa-DIA can be run on a Linux workstation or a cluster compute node with an x86-64 processor. See below for selecting the version and parser. Container runtime Docker, Apptainer, or Singularity. Choose the runtime available on your workstation or cluster. Most analysis tools, including OpenMS, MSBooster, Percolator, EasyPQP, DIA-NN, and ProteoVault, are supplied through the configured container images. docs.text: We recommend Nextflow 24.10.6 . docs.text: The easiest way to get started is to download the latest release with all submodules . docs.text: If you prefer to work from a Git checkout, clone the repository with all nested submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:TheBoutrosLab/metapipeline-DIA.git SpectroMesa-DIA cd SpectroMesa-DIA The repository and its submodules use GitHub SSH URLs, so this command requires working GitHub SSH authentication and access to the repositories. docs.text: SpectroMesa-DIA overview SpectroMesa-DIA is designed to support most major data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics data types, including Thermo RAW ( .raw ), SCIEX SWATH ( .wiff ), and Bruker diaPASEF ( .d ), across both unfractionated and fractionated experiments. The pipeline uses Nextflow to orchestrate individual tools and analysis steps. 1 It follows a spectrum-based approach similar to FragPipe , involving database searching, peptide-spectrum match (PSM) validation, protein grouping, spectral library generation, and peptide and protein quantitation. 6 Workflow MS data files pass through conversion, while Bruker .d acquisitions pass through MS/MS reconstruction. Both routes feed search, validation, and library generation. DIA-NN quantifies converted mzML files or the original Bruker acquisitions using the resulting library. QC follows quantitation, with optional ProteoVault database assembly afterward. Major components MS data preparation For file inputs, ProteoWizard msconvert produces mzML for downstream analysis; OpenMS provides an alternative conversion route for supported formats. For Bruker diaPASEF data, diaTracer reconstructs precursor-resolved pseudo-MS/MS spectra for peptide identification. The original Bruker acquisitions are retained for quantitation rather than being replaced by those reconstructed spectra. 2 , 3 , 4 Peptide identification MSFragger searches the prepared spectra against a target-decoy protein sequence database to generate candidate peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs). Its DIA search capabilities support identification from complex DIA spectra, while the Bruker route supplies spectra reconstructed by diaTracer. These candidate identifications are then evaluated by the validation stage. 5 , 6 Identification validation and protein inference MSBooster adds features derived from predicted peptide properties, and Percolator uses them to rescore PSMs and estimate identification confidence. Protein inference then relates peptide evidence to protein groups: ProteinProphet is the default, with Fido and EPIFANY available as alternatives. 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 Spectral library generation EasyPQP combines the identified peptides with their observed spectra to build a cohort spectral library for DIA-NN. It uses the accepted PSM and peptide reports from validation, preserving the selected protein assignments. For fractionated cohorts, the workflow builds libraries by fraction and combines them while retaining fraction information. DIA quantitation Upstream protein groups are retained DIA-NN is used for quantitation only, with its protein inference disabled by default. It quantifies peptides and proteins using the generated spectral library while retaining the protein groups assigned upstream by ProteinProphet , Fido , or EPIFANY . DIA-NN receives converted mzML files for the file-input route and the original .d acquisitions for the Bruker route; fractionated analyses run quantitation by fraction and aggregate the results into sample-level reports and abundance matrices. 12 Quality control The DIA QC pipeline uses pyOpenMS and dedicated summary scripts to examine acquisition data, search and validation results, protein inference, the spectral library, and DIA-NN quantitation. Cohort QC tables and interactive MS1 plots help inspect signal quality and variation across samples and fractions; Bruker acquisition QC uses the original .d data. 2 Results database ProteoVault optionally combines the DIA-NN report, protein sequence database, and cohort QC results into a validated DuckDB database. This provides a common entry point for querying the cohort alongside the published library and quantitative outputs. Database assembly is currently available for the ProteinProphet, Fido, and EPIFANY routes. The generated DuckDB database can be imported and analyzed in R using ProteoVaultR . docs.text: Understanding results SpectroMesa-DIA produces quantitative tables, quality-control summaries, and identification results. By default, it also assembles a ProteoVault database that you can explore in R. Start by checking the QC summaries, then choose the quantitative table that matches your analysis question. The main output directory is: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>/main_workflow/ Within it, results are grouped into versioned directories. The * in the paths below stands for the software version recorded in your run. To find… Look under… Quantitative reports and matrices quantitate-ProteomicDIA-*/<dataset_id>/output/DIA-NN/ QC summaries and plots qc-ProteomicDIA-*/<dataset_id>/output/ Validated identifications and protein groups validate-ProteomicPSM-*/ Original search results search-ProteomicDIA-*/ The ProteoVault database is published separately, as shown in Analyze the results with ProteoVaultR . Quantitation tables Choose a matrix For most protein-level comparisons, start with the protein-group matrix . Use precursor or peptide tables when your question requires more detail. File Rows represent Values represent <dataset_id>-report.pg_matrix.tsv Protein groups Protein-group abundance estimates. <dataset_id>-report.pr_matrix.tsv Precursors: a peptide sequence with a particular modification state and charge Normalized precursor quantities. <dataset_id>-report.modified_peptide_matrix.tsv Modified peptide sequences, with charge states combined Summed precursor quantities; generated for fractionated analyses. <dataset_id>-report.stripped_peptide_matrix.tsv Peptide sequences, with modifications and charge states combined Summed precursor quantities; generated for fractionated analyses. The identifying columns describe each row; the remaining columns hold quantities for individual samples or runs. Use acquisitions.tsv in the same directory to match acquisition names to the sample_name values in your input CSV. Fractionated matrices use sample names directly, with one quantity column per sample. Technical replicates remain separate only when you gave them distinct sample names. These are abundance measurements, not differential-abundance test results or absolute protein concentrations. Blank cells indicate missing quantities. Keep missing values distinct from measured zeros when preparing a matrix for downstream analysis. A protein-group row can represent several proteins Protein groups are assigned upstream by ProteinProphet, Fido, or EPIFANY and retained by DIA-NN under the default configuration. A group quantity does not establish a separate abundance for every member of that group. Preserve the group identifiers when joining results to annotations. Unfractionated analyses retain DIA-NN's native quantitative outputs. Fractionated analyses produce combined matrices as described below. DIA-NN's output documentation explains the native report and matrix conventions; the exact output depends on the DIA-NN version and settings used in your run. Inspect the detailed report <dataset_id>-report.tsv provides precursor observations and their associated protein groups, quantities, scores, and other measurements. It is useful when you need to investigate an individual peptide, inspect filtering, or build a custom summary. Column How to read it Run The acquisition or sample associated with the observation. Precursor.Id The precursor identifier. Protein.Group The assigned protein group. Modified.Sequence , Stripped.Sequence , Precursor.Charge The peptide's modification state, unmodified sequence, and charge. Precursor.Quantity , Precursor.Normalised Precursor quantities before and after normalization. PG.Quantity , PG.Normalised , PG.MaxLFQ Different protein-group abundance summaries. Use one consistent measure for a comparison. Q.Value , PG.Q.Value Precursor and protein-group confidence measures. These describe identification confidence, not differential-abundance significance. Protein-group quantities can be repeated on multiple precursor rows. Use the protein-group matrix for group-level comparisons rather than summing those repeated values. A report and its matrices may contain different sets of entries because their filtering rules differ. Review quality control Open <dataset_id>_QC_metrics.tsv in the QC output directory for a combined summary. Each row records a metric, its value and unit, and the sample or cohort it describes. layer identifies the analysis stage; sample_name and fraction_id indicate which acquisition or sample the metric belongs to. A blank sample name can indicate a cohort-wide metric. Before comparing abundances, review: Acquisition quality: signal distributions, scan counts, and the MS1 plots. Look for acquisitions that differ markedly from otherwise comparable samples or fractions. Identification results: search and validated identification counts, mass-error summaries, and available PSM feature distributions. Large changes can help identify acquisitions or search settings that need investigation. Quantitation: quantified precursor and protein-group counts, quantity distributions, and missingness across comparable samples. Interpret differences alongside the experimental design. Different biological samples or fractions may have different signal and identification counts without indicating a failed run. Unavailable QC values are not zero A metric marked status=unavailable could not be calculated from the available information. Do not treat it as a measured zero. Some optional measurements are omitted when their source information is absent. Interactive MS1 plots are under: mzML/<sample_name>/<fraction_id>/<sample_name>_<fraction_id>_MS1_landscape.html Open these HTML files in a browser; they work offline. They display a selection of strong MS1 peaks, rather than every recorded peak. Colors show intensity percentiles within each acquisition, so the same color does not indicate the same absolute intensity in different samples. Interpret fractionated experiments For fractionated data, DIA-NN quantifies each fraction separately. The final tables combine the accepted precursor observations across fractions, so the matrices have one quantity column per sample rather than one per fraction. Repeated precursor quantities are summed across observed fractions. Modified-peptide and stripped-peptide quantities are then summed from those precursor quantities. Protein-group MaxLFQ estimates are recalculated from the combined precursor quantities using the DIA-NN R package; they are not obtained by summing the fraction-level PG.MaxLFQ values. No additional intensity scaling is applied between fractions. Use <dataset_id>-report.fraction_coverage.tsv to inspect the observed precursor coverage and signal for each sample/fraction pair. The accompanying acquisitions.tsv preserves the mapping back to the original acquisitions. Acquisition QC remains fraction-specific, while the final quantitation QC is sample-level. Some report fields describe one representative fraction The combined report retains scores, retention times, q-values, and other fields that cannot meaningfully be summed from a representative observation with the lowest precursor q-value. Representative.Fraction.ID identifies that fraction, and Uncombined.Fields.Scope labels these fields. The retained q-values are not newly calculated across fractions. The fractionated protein-group matrix uses the pipeline's combined MaxLFQ estimates. Keep this distinction in mind when comparing it with native DIA-NN outputs from an unfractionated experiment. Fraction-specific DIA-NN reports remain in the Nextflow work directory; the published report is the combined sample-level result. Identification results Validated identifications are available as filtered idXML and mzTab files under each sample's validation output directory. Use these when inspecting the spectra and PSMs supporting an identification. Unfiltered files are also retained for specific processing steps, so choose the filtered results when you need the final accepted identification set. The selected protein-grouping method also produces cohort outputs under <dataset_id>/<method>/output/ within the validation directory. Use its protein-group results to inspect the assignments underlying your quantitation. Analyze the results with ProteoVaultR ProteoVault database assembly is enabled by default. The generated DuckDB file is located at: <output_dir>/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/<dataset_id>.proteovault.duckdb The database brings together the imported quantitative measurements, protein sequences, and QC summaries. ProteoVaultR provides read-only access from R, with functions for querying results, extracting matrices, plotting QC, and preparing downstream analyses. Follow its repository instructions to install the package, then open your database: library(ProteoVaultR) vault <- open_vault( path = "/project/results/SpectroMesa-DIA-<version>/human_dia_cohort.proteovault.duckdb" ) vault_info(vault) list_vault_tables(vault) counts <- summarize_quantified_counts(vault) protein_abundance <- matrix_protein_abundance(vault) precursor_abundance <- matrix_precursor_abundance(vault) close_vault(vault) Replace the example path, including <version> , with your database's actual location. The extracted matrices have features in rows and samples in columns. By default, the matrix functions use imported matrix measurements when available; they do not apply an additional normalization or transformation. Missing combinations remain NA . Use the ProteoVaultR analysis guides for sample metadata, QC plots, and differential-abundance analysis. Keep your experimental design and replicate assignments alongside the quantitative data when preparing comparisons.

docs.text: Running the tests The integration tests run SpectroMesa-DIA on small reference datasets to check that the analysis completes in your computing environment. You will need the installed pipeline, the public test data, the required search software, and UCLA NFTest . Start with one case before trying the other acquisition and protein-grouping routes. Install the test tools Complete the pipeline installation , including its submodules, Java, Nextflow, and the container runtime you will use. The test launcher also needs Python 3.8 or newer and UCLA NFTest ( uclahs-cds/tool-NFTest ) . You can keep the Python tools in a dedicated environment: python3 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/spectromesa-tests" source "$HOME/.venvs/spectromesa-tests/bin/activate" python3 -m pip install \ "git+https://github.com/uclahs-cds/tool-NFTest.git" \ PyYAML python-dotenv python3 -m nftest --help Activate this environment whenever you run a test, including inside a cluster job. The launcher uses NFTest from the same Python environment as python3 . Use the tested Nextflow settings: export NXF_VER=24.10.6 export NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 The Bruker reconstruction step selects its own Nextflow runtime automatically, as explained in Installation . Download the test data The Boutros Lab public S3 location is s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/ . SpectroMesa fixtures are under spectromesa/ . Install the AWS CLI if aws is not already available. Choose a data directory outside the pipeline installation. The following commands download the database and E. coli DIA fixtures needed for the E. coli cases: export TEST_DATA_DIR=/project/test-data/spectromesa mkdir -p "$TEST_DATA_DIR" aws s3 sync \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/database/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/database/" --no-sign-request aws s3 sync \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/ecoli_dia/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/ecoli_dia/" --no-sign-request For the diaPASEF case, also download: aws s3 sync \ s3://boutroslab-public/test-data/spectromesa/hela_diapasef/ \ "$TEST_DATA_DIR/hela_diapasef/" --no-sign-request --no-sign-request allows these public downloads without AWS credentials. You can rerun the sync commands to retrieve missing or updated files. Keep the folder names and the contents of each Bruker .d directory intact. Set TEST_DATA_DIR to the directory containing database/ , ecoli_dia/ , and, when downloaded, hela_diapasef/ . Do not point it to the directory above spectromesa/ . Add the required software and database settings Obtain MSFragger and diaTracer separately, following the links in Installation . The test configurations expect these paths: File or directory under TEST_DATA_DIR Needed for MSFragger-4.4.1.jar Every case listed below diaTracer-2.2.1.jar The diaPASEF case MSFragger-4.4.1/ext/bruker/ The diaPASEF case; must contain libtimsdata-2-21-0-4.so The public data download does not install these tools. Place the separately obtained files at the expected paths, or update the corresponding paths in the test configuration you plan to use. Use the public E. coli database The current E. coli test configurations name an older FASTA that is not in the public download. Before running an E. coli case, update its test/<test-case>/test.config to use the published database and matching markers below. The diaPASEF case already points to its published human database. Replace the database settings inside the existing params block of each E. coli case you intend to run: decoy_database = "${TEST_DATA_DIR}/database/UP000000625_83333-FragPipe/2026-11-12-decoys-contam-input.fasta.fas" decoy_string = 'DECOY_' decoy_position = 'prefix' contam_string = 'contam_' contam_position = 'prefix' The case configuration already reads TEST_DATA_DIR from the environment. Keep its setup statements and final methods.setup() call. Changing the database path alone is insufficient: its decoy marker must also match. Configure the test environment The test launcher reads .env and nftest.yml from the pipeline installation directory. Run the test commands from that directory, while keeping the downloaded data and generated results elsewhere. Normal analyses can continue to use the separate analysis-directory layout . If the installation does not already have a .env file, create one from the template: cd /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA cp .env-template .env Edit the existing file if you have already configured it. For the bundled AWS test setup, use: NXF_VER=24.10.6 NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1 TEST_DATA_DIR=/project/test-data/spectromesa NFT_CLUSTER=boutroslab_aws NFT_RUN_ROOT=/scratch/your_user/spectromesa-tests Use full paths accessible from the compute node. The launcher loads .env with precedence over exported shell values, so update this file when changing the data path or cluster selection. NFT_CLUSTER Runtime and resource plan Location of test runs boutroslab_aws Docker; 32 CPUs and 128 GB memory NFT_RUN_ROOT/<SLURM_JOB_ID>/ ; requires an active Slurm job pines Apptainer; 64 CPUs and 500 GB memory NFT_RUN_ROOT/ Empty Docker with the AWS resource plan NFT_RUN_ROOT/ ; no Slurm job-ID requirement These are the supplied test configurations, not resource reservations. For another environment, adapt the case's runtime and resource settings using the configuration guide . Launch inside your compute allocation On a cluster, obtain an allocation matching the selected resource plan before running the test. The launcher does not submit a job for you. NFT_CLUSTER=boutroslab_aws checks for SLURM_JOB_ID and stops if it is absent. For Apptainer, you can also set the image-cache variables described in Installation in .env to reuse downloaded images between tests. Run a test case With the Python environment active and your compute allocation ready, start with the E. coli mzML case: cd /path/to/SpectroMesa-DIA python3 test/run-nftest.py test_integration_MSFragger_ProteinProphet_DIANN Choose another case by replacing the final argument: Test case What it exercises test_integration_MSFragger_ProteinProphet_DIANN E. coli mzML input, MSFragger, ProteinProphet grouping, and DIA-NN quantitation test_integration_MSFragger_Epifany_DIANN The E. coli mzML workflow with EPIFANY grouping test_integration_MSFragger_ProteinProphet_DIANN_multifraction Two E. coli samples with three fractions each, including fraction-aware library generation and quantitation aggregation test_integration_MSConvert_MSFragger_ProteinProphet_DIANN Two E. coli Thermo RAW files, including conversion before searching test_integration_diaTracer_MSFragger_ProteinProphet_DIANN A HeLa Bruker diaPASEF acquisition, including reconstruction for search and quantitation from the original .d data All cases listed here also run QC and build the ProteoVault results database. These are integration runs using the actual analysis tools, so they take longer than a configuration check. The current cases check pipeline execution; they do not define numerical assertions for expected identification counts or intensities. Check results and investigate failures The launcher prints the selected case, work directory, and output root before NFTest starts. Check its completion message and exit status, then inspect the published outputs using Understanding results . The resolved run root is NFT_RUN_ROOT , with the Slurm job-ID directory added for boutroslab_aws : <run-root>/ <test-case>/ Published analysis results .nftest-temp/<case-id>/ Test launch files and temporary work Temporary files are retained by the supplied test settings. If a case fails, keep them while inspecting the NFTest log, .nextflow.log , and the failed task's command logs. Common setup problems are a mismatched TEST_DATA_DIR , a missing JAR, a database path or marker that does not match the downloaded FASTA, or a container runtime unavailable on the compute node. The test launcher does not add -resume . Rerunning a case should not be assumed to resume the failed analysis; see the resume guide for the separate analysis workflow.

docs.text: Spectral library generation EasyPQP combines validated identification evidence and measured spectra into the library used by DIA-NN for quantitation. Protein labels come from the upstream grouping method. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Match each sample’s validated idXML to its mzML acquisitions. For samples with multiple fractions, OpenMS IDRipper separates the identification records by source acquisition. Prepare an EasyPQP-compatible idXML using Percolator posterior error probabilities, then extract the corresponding PSM and fragment-peak information. Build the library using the accepted PSM and peptide reports from validation. These reports determine the accepted evidence and protein labels. For fractionated experiments, build a library for each fraction_id across samples, label its rows by fraction, and combine the fraction libraries into one TSV for quantitation . Inputs and outputs All inputs are supplied automatically: mzML acquisitions, validated idXML files, and the cohort PSM and peptide reports. The main output is the EasyPQP TSV used by the next step, with a SHA-512 checksum. Optional intermediate files can help investigate a failed library build. Use the same fraction_id for corresponding fractions across samples. mzML basenames must be unique across the experiment and must not contain extra dots; see Preparing inputs . The score is selected for you SpectroMesa-DIA sets idxml_score_type to Posterior Error Probability for the documented validation routes, and easypqp_score_type already defaults to PEP . docs.text: DIA quantitation DIA-NN is used for quantitation. It measures peptides and proteins using the generated spectral library. Protein inference is disabled by default, so the protein groups assigned by ProteinProphet, Fido, or EPIFANY are retained. Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Prepare the EasyPQP TSV for DIA-NN, validating and expanding the fragment annotations without changing the source library. Analyze all samples together for each fraction, using mzML acquisitions or the original Bruker .d directories. For an unfractionated cohort, retain DIA-NN’s native report and quantitation matrices. For a fractionated cohort, combine confident normalized precursor observations across fractions, sum repeated precursor quantities within each sample, and calculate sample-level protein-group quantities with diann_maxlfq() from the DIA-NN R package. The fractionated calculation does not apply extra cross-fraction intensity scaling. Its protein-group quantities are calculated by the aggregation step and should not be described as DIA-NN’s native QuantUMS output. Inputs and outputs SpectroMesa-DIA supplies the acquisition manifest and the generated EasyPQP library. Bruker quantitation uses the original .d data, not the reconstructed search spectra. Outputs are the cohort report, precursor matrix, protein-group matrix, and quantitation logs. Final matrices contain one quantity column per sample_name , including experiments with multiple fractions. See Understanding results . Keep the upstream protein groups no_prot_inf already defaults to true . Leave it true: setting it to false allows DIA-NN to perform protein inference and changes the grouping strategy. docs.text: Prepare the EasyPQP TSV for DIA-NN, validating and expanding the fragment annotations without changing the source library. Analyze all samples together for each fraction, using mzML acquisitions or the original Bruker .d directories. For an unfractionated cohort, retain DIA-NN’s native report and quantitation matrices. For a fractionated cohort, combine confident normalized precursor observations across fractions, sum repeated precursor quantities within each sample, and calculate sample-level protein-group quantities with diann_maxlfq() from the DIA-NN R package. The fractionated calculation does not apply extra cross-fraction intensity scaling. Its protein-group quantities are calculated by the aggregation step and should not be described as DIA-NN’s native QuantUMS output.

docs.text: Database search MSFragger-DIA searches each mzML acquisition against the target-decoy FASTA. It identifies candidate peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), which are scored and filtered in the validation step . Open the original flowchart at full size . How it works Write a native MSFragger parameter file from your search settings. Search each acquisition or fraction independently, producing pepXML and PIN results. Convert the reported peptide ranks to idXML and combine the ranks for each acquisition. Merge fractions sharing the same sample_name into a sample-level identification file for validation. The search retains candidate matches for statistical validation. A search hit is not yet an accepted identification. Inputs and outputs Inputs are the prepared mzML files, your target-decoy FASTA, and the separately obtained MSFragger JAR. SpectroMesa-DIA supplies all three from earlier steps and the shared configuration. Outputs include per-acquisition pepXML and PIN files and one combined idXML per sample. These provide the identification evidence for MSBooster and Percolator. Sample names define the validation unit Fractions with the same sample_name are combined before sample-level FDR estimation. Give technical replicates distinct sample names when you want separate validation and quantitation columns. See Preparing inputs . docs.text: PSM validation and protein grouping MSBooster and Percolator rescore the search results, and OpenMS estimates PSM q-values for each sample. ProteinProphet then groups proteins across the cohort by default; Fido and EPIFANY are alternatives. Those groups are carried into the spectral library and retained during quantitation. Open the original flowchart at full size . The original diagram also includes standalone analysis routes. The steps below describe the route used by SpectroMesa-DIA. How it works Match peptide sequences to the target-decoy FASTA with PeptideIndexer, checking their protein associations and target/decoy labels. Export PSM features, add MSBooster prediction-based features, and run Percolator. Import its posterior error probabilities (PEPs) into the identification files. Estimate sample-level PSM q-values and filter the identification output. The default maximum q-value is 0.01 . Use the unfiltered rescored evidence across samples to infer protein groups. ProteinProphet uses an iProphet/ProteinProphet route; Fido and EPIFANY use their respective probabilistic grouping methods. Export accepted PSMs and peptide-to-protein-group assignments for library generation . This export has its own PSM q-value cutoff, also 0.01 by default. The filtered idXML and mzTab outputs help you inspect accepted identifications. The library export combines the q-value-qualified PSM evidence with the selected cohort protein groups; it is not simply a conversion of the filtered idXML file. Inputs and outputs Inputs are sample-level search idXML files, the matching mzML acquisitions, and the same FASTA used for searching. SpectroMesa-DIA prepares their manifests automatically. Outputs include rescored identification evidence, filtered idXML and mzTab files, cohort protein groups, EasyPQP PSM and peptide reports, and an export summary. See Understanding results for the files most useful to inspect. A group probability is not an FDR cutoff proteinprophet_min_probability is already 0.0 ; fido_min_probability and epifany_min_probability are 0.01 . These are minimum group probabilities for export. A value of 0.01 does not mean a 1% protein-group FDR. Validation settings Set parameters inside validate_ProteomicPSM . Only the chosen grouping method’s probability settings apply. SpectroMesa-DIA fixes the rescoring route to MSBooster plus Percolator and disables multi-engine consensus. Settings for the standalone OpenMS Percolator or consensus routes are listed separately and have no effect on this workflow.
